Stacked co-packaged Si-Ge-Si photodetectors 
with > 60 GHz bandwidth for near-infrared 
wavelength-simulation
E. P. Devine1,2*, Toshishige Yamada1,3, Shih-Yuan Wang1 and M. Saif Islam2
1  Introduction
The demand for efficient, high-speed vertically illuminated photodetectors (PDs) and 
high-speed co-packaged optics for various applications, including hyperscale data cen­
ters, AI and high performance computing systems, optical networks, lidar applications, 
and imaging [1–3], drives research toward innovative approaches, such as photon-trap­
ping for photodetectors [4] or, equivalently, the use of “dressed” photons [5] and image 
sensors [6]. While silicon photonics produces compact, multifunctional, and low-power 
photonic circuits built on the same chip, many applications need near-infrared wave­
lengths that can be achieved with group IV elements. Silicon-germanium (Si–Ge) pho­
todetectors [7–10] are addressing these needs in optical communications. Recently, 
progress has been made in developing more efficient and faster photodetectors using 
Discover Electronics
Abstract
We present a multistack design of ultra-thin germanium-on-silicon (Ge-on-Si) 
photodetectors (PDs) featuring both backside-illuminated (BSI) and top-illuminated 
architectures, optimized for operation in the 1.0–1.4 μm wavelength range. Using 
Monte Carlo molecular dynamics simulations, we evaluate the effects of doping 
profiles and biasing on device performance. A Ge absorption layer with a thickness 
of 350 nm enables high-speed operation exceeding 60 GHz, while nanostructures 
integrated at the bottom of the Ge layer enhance optical absorption efficiency to 
as high as 80%. The BSI design supports vertical integration with electronic wafers, 
facilitating compact, low-latency signal processing and transmission—particularly 
beneficial for optical interconnects in data centers and other high-performance 
computing environments. We also perform a comparative analysis of BSI and 
top-illuminated designs, highlighting the performance trade-offs and integration 
advantages in high-speed, vertically stacked, co-packaged optics. These results offer a 
compact, CMOS (Complementary Metal-Oxide-Semiconductor) -compatible solution 
for high-speed optical interconnects in future hyperscale data centers.
Keywords  High-speed photodetectors, Multistack co-packaging, Optical receivers, 
Co-package optics, Hyperscale datacenters

micro- and nanostructures in Si and Ge, as well as in III-V semiconductor materials [11], 
for short [12] and mid-infrared [13] wavelengths. The interest in Ge PDs remains high, 
as they offer versatile solutions for near-infrared applications that require eye safety. The 
ultra-thin active layer in PD drastically increases its speed for the vertically illuminated 
device, as the electrons and holes have much shorter paths. Another aspect of achieving 
high-speed co-packaging lies in the architecture that reduces losses and signal distortion 
due to dispersion and reflection in the circuit, such as a multistack co-packaged optics 
[14–16]. We propose a stack design that can be part of a multistack co-package optics, 
significantly increasing the bandwidth. BSI designs offer several advantages, including 
reduced device footprint, improved alignment with optical packaging, and simplified 
electrical routing through front-side contacts. These attributes make BSI geometries 
particularly attractive for co-packaged optics, where vertical integration with driver 
electronics is critical to minimizing latency and interconnect parasitic effects. Although 
the lateral high-speed Ge PDs were [17], it was challenging to achieve high-speed back­
side-illuminated BSI design. The pulse amplitude modulation (PAM-4) technique allows 
for exceeding the rate reported in [10, 14]. Reducing the size of the PD also enhances 
speed, potentially at the expense of efficiency.
It was shown in [4] that the micro-holes on the top of the device reduce reflection 
and produce modes that stay in the active layer longer, significantly increasing photon 
absorption. We propose a Ge-on-Si structure with holes at the bottom of the Ge active 
layer. The fabrication of this structure is feasible using stacked Complementary Metal-
Oxide-Semiconductor (CMOS) technology [14, 15]. This design benefits electronics by 
allowing them to be stacked on the same wafer close to the chip contacts, thereby reduc­
ing transmission line losses. The multi-stack p-i-n PD enables ultrahigh-speed, low-
latency, cost-effective, and energy-efficient communication systems [16]. The goal of this 
study is to identify an optimal vertically illuminated Ge PD design that strikes a balance 
between quantum efficiency and device speed by utilizing light-trapping structures. Our 
design also leverages the multi-stack p-i-n PD technology. The multi-stack technology 
utilizes epi layers that can be stacked on top of each other, with contacts in both the top 
and bottom layers, along with a transparent window for light. This arrangement brings 
the electron-hole generation closer to the other electronics on the chip, allowing for a 
reduction in the length of the electrical transmission lines and a decrease in the losses 
associated with them.
The schematics of the PD and its incorporation into the PIC are shown in Fig. 1. The 
upper Si layer measures 100 nm, with 50 nm of p-doped Si and 50 nm of p-doped Ge. 
The active Ge layer is only 350 nm thick, followed by 100 nm of n-doped Ge and 25 nm 
of n-doped Si, allowing holes to pass through the Si and Ge layers. All the PD compo­
nents are placed on the SiO2 layer, as illustrated in Fig. 1(a). The electrodes are arranged 
at the top and bottom of the PD. The electrodes have a transparent window for light 
illumination. The upper Si layer includes an antireflection (AR) structure that minimizes 
reflection in the wavelength range of 1000 to 1400 nm.
We studied a variety of micro-hole configurations Fig. 1(b): cylindrical holes of differ­
ent sizes ranging from 200 nm to 1000 nm, periods from 300 to 1200 nm, and depths 
from 50 to 200 nm in a square lattice. Additionally, we examined composite holes that 
form a cluster of 7 holes in a hexagonal lattice, creating a larger hole Fig. 1(c). The com­
posite holes create a square lattice similar to the structure with holes shown in Fig. 1(b).

2  Optimization for the ge photodetector
The efficiency and bandwidth of the Ge photodetector were modeled in two steps. First, 
the Finite Difference Time Domain (FDTD) simulations [19] for the optical field are 
presented. The absorbed light is calculated by taking the integral of the Poynting vector 
that enters and exits the volume [4]. The incident light was perpendicular to the sur­
face. Perfect Matching Layers (PML) were used at the boundaries perpendicular to the 
light’s incident direction, and periodic boundaries were applied to the other boundaries. 
The second part involves electrical simulations that model electron-hole transport and 
resulting photocurrent. We used a Monte-Carlo simulation [19–21] to simulate the cur­
rent in the photodetector. The simulation technique was verified with the experimental 
data provided by [7] for Monte-Carlo simulations. The comparison of simulations and 
experimental data for the structure from [7] is provided in Table 1. The FDTD simula­
tions were verified with data from [7].

We optimized the photodetector for a wide wavelength range of 1 to 1.4 microns. It 
was observed in [8] that the optimal micro-holes for trapping photons in the Ge layer 
were 1000–1200 nm and the period 1200–1500 nm. The smaller holes produced sharp 
guided resonance. However, the combination of several resonances that are close to 
each other is possible and can produce a strong absorption across a wide range of wave­
lengths. We also studied the option to use composite holes that combine the smaller 
holes into a structure with a diameter of 1000–1200 nm.
The Monte Carlo simulations demonstrated that the shape of the micro-holes can 
influence electron-hole transport and, consequently, the speed of the device. One issue 
is surface recombination, but it can be mitigated with proper passivation [22]. We place 
our holes at the bottom, which is filled with silicon oxide, thereby providing effective 
passivation. This allows us to assume that surface recombination is minimal. The second 
issue is that the holes act as obstacles between the electrodes, causing carriers to become 
trapped in the areas near the bottom of the micro-holes. This creates charges that slow 
down the current and result in a tail. Eventually, the carriers will either recombine or 
move out of the area due to drift in the reverse-biased PDs. Reducing the micro-hole 
size lowers the area of slowdown for the carriers, see Fig. 2(d). The third concern is the 
doping and the width of the n and p regions. We have observed that relatively small (50–
100 nm, see Fig. 1) and highly doped n- and p-type regions generate a stronger field, thus 
decreasing the response time. These regions are thin (100 nm), with both n and p doping 
concentrations at 1019 cm− 3. The simulations provided the distribution of electrons and 
holes, the built-in voltage for a given doping concentration, as well as the potential under 
reverse or forward bias. The current response to a light pulse was simulated with reverse 
bias.

For optimal design, we conducted simulations for various thicknesses of the Ge 
absorbing layer and sizes of the PD. The Ge thickness varied from 100 nm to 500 nm, 
and we used diameters of 1, 2, and 30 microns. The extremely small PD can be utilized 
with multicore fibers. The PD with a 1 micron side had only one smaller composite hole, 
shown in Fig. 1(c, d). The previous simulations for Ge [7] indicated that micro-holes 
can significantly enhance optical absorption with diameters ranging from 1000 to 1200 
nm. We aim to utilize smaller holes to create a structure with an approximate diam­
eter of 1200 nm. Figure 1(a-d) shows the unit cell of the microhole structure lattice. We 
employed 300 nm diameter nanoholes, spaced 400 nm apart in the center. For the 1 μm 
size device, only one composite hole with a diameter of 800 nm was used. The composite 
hole consisted of 6 holes of 200 nm diameter each, and a distance of 300 nm between the 
centers.
The results are shown in Fig. 2(a) for the regular holes on the bottom of Ge (red line) 
and the structures made of randomized holes (Fig. 1(d)) with a diameter of 300 ± 100 
nm and a distance of 400 ± 50 nm. The composite nano-holes produce absorption com­
parable to that of optimal cylindrical micro-holes at the bottom. The results were com­
pared with a flat device (black dashed line). The improvement in all cases is significant; 
however, the randomization helped smooth out the resonances. Even better results are 
achieved by using microstructures in the Si layer on top to minimize reflection. The 
randomization of the composite micro-holes in the top layer did not yield a significant 
improvement. In contrast, both configurations produced absorption between 60 and 
80%, which is better than 1-micron periodic micro-holes for most wavelengths between 
1 and 1.4 microns. We chose this range due to its best application potential. The micro-
nano-holes help increase efficiency in the longer wavelength region, up to 1.8 microns, 
although the optimal micro-hole parameters for this region need to be simulated. The 
comparison of the efficiency of a large hole, a composite hole, and randomized holes 
is shown in Fig. 2(a) with the black solid curve. All light-trapping structures enhance 
efficiency compared to a flat device. The larger holes exhibit guided resonances that 
improve efficiency in a narrow range of wavelengths. The composed and primarily ran­
domized holes provide enhanced efficiency over a broader range of wavelengths, result­
ing in smoother peaks. The optical intensity distribution shows the typical variations in 
lateral direction (see Fig. 2(c)).
However, the large micro-hole can distort the potential created by the backward bias 
and slow down the electrons and holes, resulting in a longer tail in the pulse response. 
Due to the low electric field regions beneath the holes, the tail in the pulse response 
is higher for the larger hole. The fast Fourier transformation (FFT) of the current J is 
shown in Fig. 2b. Although the width of the pulse is short because the active layer is thin, 
the tail affects the bandwidth. The bandwidth at 3 dB for the composite micro-holes is 
approximately 60 GHz, while for the large hole, it is only about 40 GHz.
The data center’s applications could benefit from fast and compact photodetectors 
(PDs) incorporated into the photonic circuits with multicore fiber. The size of the PDs 
could be as small as 5 microns and even smaller. We optimized the bandwidth vs. effi­
ciency for PDs with a side of 30, 5, 2, and 1 microns. We assume that the beam was 
focused on the PD surface without losses due to the size of the PD, and all the coupling 
losses are determined by reflection. The results are shown in Fig. 3. The maximum band­
width can exceed 70 GHz, with an efficiency of 40%. The optimal Ge thickness can be

found as a trade-off between the bandwidth and efficiency. While a 30 micron PD size 
can achieve a maximum efficiency of about 80% with a bandwidth of 60 GHz, a smaller 
PD size with a thinner Ge layer provides a bandwidth up to 70 GHz. The full benefits of 
the fast PD can be utilized in the stack co-package that the PD is compatible with. Small-
sized devices have a smaller capacity and wider bandwidth. However, at a size signifi­
cantly smaller than 30 microns, the other effects, like time and velocity of carrier transit 
across the absorption layer, parasitic capacitance, and package inductance, have more 
influence on the bandwidth.
3  Simulations for PD in stack co-package
The high-speed Ge PD can be particularly advantageous in photonic circuits with low 
losses and low dispersion, resulting in speeds exceeding 60 Gbps. The proposed design 
is compatible with the stack co-package and benefits from shorter transmission lines 
with low losses and reduced dispersion. The stack co-package for the PD is illustrated 
in Fig. 1f. One more advantage compared to the side-by-side design is the ability to use 
a shorter asymmetric coplanar line without a bend. This coplanar line can be as short as 
10 microns, while the microstrip length for the side-by-side configuration can reach up 
to 5 mm. Speed limitations arise from the pulse width and the tail of the pulse response, 
estimating the 3 dB bandwidth at approximately 60–70 GHz. Additionally, the asymmet­
ric coplanar connection between the PD and other devices on the chip may incur losses 
and dispersion, which could affect the overall speed. The eye diagrams were simulated 
using Cadence. Longer transmission lines experience greater losses, dispersion, parasitic 
capacitance, and inductance. Moreover, bends in the microstrip lead to reflections.
The eye diagram (Fig. 4) was generated for a pulse simulated for a PD with a 30-micron 
size and a 350-nm Ge thickness, analyzing both multistack and side-by-side ICs across 
various bit rates from 10 to 60 Gbps. We used 10 5 signal samples for the simulations. 
The eye diagram opening correlates with the bit rate error (BER). As expected, a smaller 
eye opening corresponds to a higher bit rate. Notably, in the 60 Gbps stack PIC, the eye

opening is significantly larger than that for side-by-side coplanar lengths of 2.5 and 5 
mm (Fig. 3). The eye opening is defined as the ratio of the height of the clear area at the 
center to the total height. For the 60 GHz rate, this ratio is approximately 0.35 for a mul­
tistack design, reduced to 0.15 for a side-by-side configuration with a 2.5 mm coplanar, 
and less than 0.1 for a 5 mm coplanar.
The numerical representation of the quality of the signal is the eye-diagram height, 
which is the difference between the mean “1” and the mean “0”. The Q-factor, the ratio of 
the height to the sum of the noise standard deviation for “1” and “0”, is Q = 7 for 40 GHz 
and Q = 5 for 60 GHz for 10 mm coplanar, and Q = 4.5 and 3 for the same bit rates for 1 
mm coplanar, and even lower for 5 mm coplanar.
Assuming that the edges of the eye diagram follow a Gaussian distribution, we can 
estimate the width of this distribution from the simulations, subsequently allowing us 
to estimate the bit rate error. In our model, we assume that the noise consists of ther­
mal, shot, and intersymbol interference components and could range from 1.5 to 3.5 µA, 
depending on the bit rate for the coplanar length of 10 μm. For the 1 mW optical power, 
the photocurrent is about 0.7 mA and the signal-to-noise ratio is 0.003 to 0.006. Besides 
noise, we took into account jitter and dispersion typical for the design. The BER for the 
stack co-package design is up to 10− 12, whereas the long coplanar configuration can sig­
nificantly increase the BER. The high bandwidth facilitates a high-speed co-packaged 
PD that supports 60–70 Gbps, with potential for further increases through modulation 
techniques. The state-of-the-art parameters are summarized in Table 2 for vertically illu­

The PDs with better bandwidth are not CMOS compatible and reported lower quan­
tum efficiency. The pulse amplitude modulation (PAM4) technique [10] permits dou­
bling the bit rate, achieving a rate of 120–140 Gbps, which surpasses recent reports.
4  Conclusion
This work demonstrates that incorporating nanostructured holes at the bottom of the 
active Ge layer significantly enhances both quantum efficiency and bandwidth in thin 
Ge photodetectors across a broad wavelength range. Simulation results indicate that 
bandwidths of 60–70 GHz can be achieved for vertically illuminated devices, enabling 
data rates up to 140 Gbps when combined with advanced modulation techniques. The 
optimized Ge layer thickness of 350 nm, along with thin, highly doped p- and n-regions,

contributes to faster carrier transport and improved device speed. Our study also shows 
that randomized composite micro-hole designs enhance quantum absorption over 
a wider spectral range compared to traditional approaches that rely on narrowband 
guided-mode resonances. Additionally, we examined the benefits of stack co-packaging, 
which not only supports compact integration but also reduces signal loss and dispersion. 
This architecture is particularly suitable for high-speed, energy-efficient, and low-cost 
optical interconnects using small-diameter PDs with multicore fibers, offering a scalable 
solution for next-generation data centers and communication systems.

Abstract: We present a multistack design of ultra-thin germanium-on-silicon (Ge-on-Si) photodetectors (PDs) featuring both backside-illuminated (BSI) and top-illuminated architectures, optimized for operation in the 1.0–1.4 μm wavelength range. Using Monte Carlo molecular dynamics simulations, we evaluate the effects of doping profiles and biasing on device performance. A Ge absorption layer with a thickness of 350 nm enables high-speed operation exceeding 60 GHz, while nanostructures integrated at the bottom of the Ge layer enhance optical absorption efficiency to as high as 80%. The BSI design supports vertical integration with electronic wafers, facilitating compact, low-latency signal processing and transmission—particularly beneficial for optical interconnects in data centers and other high-performance computing environments. We also perform a comparative analysis of BSI and top-illuminated designs, highlighting the performance trade-offs and integration advantages in high-speed, vertically stacked, co-packaged optics. These results offer a compact, CMOS (Complementary Metal-Oxide-Semiconductor) -compatible solution for high-speed optical interconnects in future hyperscale data centers.
